Humble
HUM-bul
v.
Latin humilis (lowly, on the ground), from humus (earth). Renders the Hebrew ‘ānāh, “to afflict, humble,” and shāphēl, “to be low”; and the Greek tapeinoō, “to make low, humble.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To humble (as a verb) is the active making-low of the proud soul—either by God’s providential dealings or by the saint’s own deliberate act of self-humbling under the mighty hand of God. The Bible uses the verb in both directions, and the two are inseparable. God humbles: He humbled Pharaoh, He humbled Nebuchadnezzar at the height of his pride until he ate grass like the oxen, He humbles every soul who exalts itself against Him—for God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble, and he that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted. The saint humbles himself: James and Peter both press the same command—humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up; humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time. The pattern of biblical humbling is therefore active and willed, not merely the slumped posture of a beaten man. The saint takes the lower seat at the feast, lest he be told to give place; he confesses his sin instead of excusing it; he yields to authority where authority is owed; he refuses the inward boast and the outward display; he reckons others better than himself, esteems them more highly; he washes feet because his Master washed feet, and he counts no service beneath him because the Son of God counted no service beneath Him. The supreme model is Christ: he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; and the supreme law is the inversion that runs through the kingdom: the way up is down, the great is the servant, the first is the last, and the humbled soul is the exalted one. Apart from active humbling, all subsequent graces wither; with it, the soul stands in the very place where God delights to give grace.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HUMBLE as to abase; to reduce to a low state; to crush; to subdue; to make submissive; in religion, to repress what is haughty in oneself and to walk softly before God.

expand to see more

HUMBLE, v.t. — 1. To abase; to reduce to a low state. 2. To crush; to subdue; to break, as the spirit or pride. 3. To make submissive; as, to humble an enemy. 4. In religion, to repress what is haughty in oneself; to lower oneself in one’s own estimation, and to walk softly before God.

HUMBLING, ppr. — Abasing; reducing to a low condition or rank; subduing pride; rendering submissive or modest.

📖 Key Scripture

James 4:10 — "Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up."

1 Peter 5:6 — "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time."

Philippians 2:8 — "And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross."

Micah 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The verb humble is corrupted by the false humility of the age—the curated self-deprecation that performs lowliness while jealously guarding the inward boast—and by the inverse pride of the assertiveness culture that despises self-humbling as weakness and refuses the inversion at the heart of the gospel.

expand to see more

The age has two characteristic corruptions of humbling, and the believer absorbs both. The first is performed false humility: the carefully curated self-deprecation, the visible token of lowliness offered up for social credit, the boast disguised as confession (‘my biggest weakness is that I work too hard’)—the form of humility without the substance, retaining the inward pride while presenting the outward posture. Scripture is sharper than this: the humbling commanded is not a performance for human view but a real lowering of the soul before God, who sees through every performance and resists the proud even when the proud have learned to perform humility well. The cure is not better performance but the actual act of self-humbling—confessing what is actually true, taking the lower seat in reality, esteeming others better in fact, refusing the inward boast that the performance was meant to mask.

The opposite and more contemporary corruption is the assertiveness culture’s active despising of self-humbling as weakness. The believer is told from every corner of the surrounding world to assert himself, to lean in, to know his worth, to never apologize, to refuse to be made small—and the gospel-shaped inversion that says he that humbleth himself shall be exalted is felt as a relic of a backward and crushing era. But the inversion is not optional Christianity; it is the inner shape of the kingdom and the imitation of the King who humbled Himself to the death of the cross. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers both the freedom and the dignity of the lower seat: the freedom from the exhausting labor of self-promotion, and the dignity of walking the road his Master walked—the road that ends not in obscurity but in exaltation, in due time, by the very hand under which the soul learned to be humbled.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ‘ānāh (to afflict, humble) and shāphēl (to be low); Greek tapeinoō (to make low, humble)—both God’s providential humbling and the saint’s active self-humbling under His mighty hand.

expand to see more

Hebrew ‘ānāh (H6031) — to afflict, humble, oppress; both God’s humbling of His people and the soul’s self-affliction.

Hebrew shāphēl (H8213) — to be low, abased, brought down.

Greek tapeinoō (G5013) — to make low, humble (James 4:10; 1 Pet 5:6; Phil 2:8).

Greek tapeinophrosunē (G5012) — lowliness of mind, humility (the noun).

Usage

"Biblical humbling is active and willed: the saint takes the lower seat in reality, not as performance, and the gospel-shaped inversion exalts him in due time."

"He humbled himself—the supreme model is Christ, who set aside the use of His prerogatives and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross."

"Curated self-deprecation and assertiveness culture corrupt the verb in opposite directions; biblical humbling is the real lowering of the soul before God who sees through both."
